title: WHY DID SOMEONE WHO TOUCHED A MENSTRUATING WOMAN’S BED HAVE TO WASH?
paragraphs: WHY DID SOMEONE WHO TOUCHED A MENSTRUATING WOMAN’S BED HAVE TO WASH?

Leviticus 15 sounds disturbing until you understand what “unclean” actually meant. Then a bleeding woman reaches for Jesus—and suddenly an ancient command becomes part of one of the most beautiful pictures of the Gospel.
There is a verse in Leviticus that many Christians quietly skip.
Not because they hate Scripture.
Because they do not know what to do with it.
It talks about menstruation.
A bed.
Someone touching that bed.
Washing clothes.
Bathing.
And being “unclean until evening.”
And if we are honest, to modern ears it can sound almost insulting.
Was God saying a menstruating woman was dirty?
Was her body somehow sinful?
Why would simply touching the place where she slept require someone to wash?
And perhaps the uncomfortable question beneath all the others is this:
What kind of God makes rules like that?
Stay with the text.
Because if you stop at the word “unclean,” you may walk away with a picture of God that the passage itself does not require.
And if you keep reading the biblical story until a desperate, bleeding woman pushes through a crowd and touches Jesus...
everything changes.
Leviticus 15:19 begins in Hebrew:
וְאִשָּׁה כִּי־תִהְיֶה זָבָה דָּם
Ve’ishah ki-tihyeh zavah dam...
In straightforward English:
“When a woman has a discharge, and her discharge is blood...”
The passage says she enters a condition described with the Hebrew word נִדָּה — niddah, associated here with her menstrual state or separation.
Then comes another important Hebrew word:
טָמֵא — tamei.
It is often translated “unclean.”
That English word can mislead us if we automatically hear:
filthy.
disgusting.
immoral.
sinful.
That is not an adequate way to understand what Leviticus is describing.
This is the world of ritual purity and impurity.
And that distinction changes everything.
The woman was not being accused of committing a sin simply because she menstruated.
Think about what surrounds this passage.
Just a few verses earlier, Leviticus says that when a man has an emission of semen, he must bathe his body and remains tamei until evening.
Clothing or leather touched by semen must be washed.
After sexual relations involving an emission, both the man and woman bathe and remain tamei until evening.
Then the text turns to menstruation.
In other words, the chapter is not singling women out as uniquely dirty.
It is dealing with bodily discharges and the ritual categories governing Israel's life before God.
That matters.
Because sometimes people have used passages like this to place shame on women that the passage itself never placed there.
God did not look at a woman experiencing the ordinary functioning of the body He created and say:
“You have sinned by being a woman.”
The text does not say that.
Now read what happens to the bed.
Leviticus 15:20 says:
וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר תִּשְׁכַּב עָלָיו בְּנִדָּתָהּ יִטְמָא
Anything on which she lies during this condition becomes tamei.
Then verse 21 says:
וְכָל־הַנֹּגֵעַ בְּמִשְׁכָּבָהּ יְכַבֵּס בְּגָדָיו וְרָחַץ בַּמַּיִם וְטָמֵא עַד־הָעָרֶב
The person touching her bedding was to wash his clothes, bathe in water, and remain tamei until evening.
Notice something easily missed.
There is no punishment here.
No beating.
No fine.
No declaration that the person has become evil.
No statement that touching the bed was itself a moral transgression.
Instead:
Wash.
Bathe.
Wait.
Evening comes.
The temporary condition ends.
That is enormously important.
The washing was part of Israel's God-given system for dealing with ritual impurity.
Israel was being taught that approaching the holy God was not casual.
Life and death mattered.
Blood mattered.
The body mattered.
Purity mattered.
Boundaries mattered.
And the presence of God in the midst of His people mattered.
Leviticus 15 eventually gives the theological concern behind these regulations: Israel was not to defile God's dwelling place in their midst.
This was not merely an ancient hygiene manual.
And we should be careful not to reduce it to one.
Washing certainly involves actual water and physical cleansing, but the chapter itself places these washings within Israel's system of ritual purity.
The purpose was larger than “God was teaching them to kill germs.”
The text is concerned with holiness.
With access.
With sacred space.
With the astonishing reality that the holy God had chosen to dwell among human beings.
And that makes what happens centuries later almost breathtaking.
Because another woman begins to bleed.
Not seven days.
Not fourteen.
Not a month.
Twelve years.
Mark tells us about her.
She had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years.
She had endured much.
She had sought help.
She had spent what she had.
And instead of becoming better, she had become worse.
Try not to read that clinically.
Imagine twelve years.
Twelve years of waking up hoping this might finally be over.
Twelve years of seeing the blood again.
Twelve years of disappointment.
Twelve years of explaining.
Twelve years of exhaustion.
Twelve years of wondering whether tomorrow will look exactly like yesterday.
And then she hears about Jesus.
A crowd surrounds Him.
People are pressing against Him.
And somewhere inside that crowd is a woman carrying twelve years of pain.
She tells herself that if she can only touch His garment, she will be healed.
Then she reaches.
Her fingers touch His clothing.
And immediately...
the bleeding stops.
But something even more beautiful happens.
Jesus stops too.
“Who touched My garments?”
The disciples are confused.
Everyone is touching You.
The crowd is pressing against You.
What do You mean, “Who touched Me?”
But Jesus keeps looking.
Until she comes trembling.
And tells Him the truth.
Imagine that moment.
She may have expected rebuke.
She may have expected exposure.
She may have expected to disappear back into the crowd as anonymously as she entered it.
Jesus would not let her leave merely knowing that her body had changed.
He wanted her to know how He saw her.
And the word He gives her is devastatingly tender:
“Daughter.”
Not nuisance.
Not contaminant.
Not embarrassment.
Not problem.
Daughter.
Then He sends her away in peace.
Do not flatten this story by pretending Mark explicitly says, “Jesus is now abolishing Leviticus 15.” Mark does not make that sentence.
But the biblical contrast is still extraordinary.
Under the Levitical purity system, bodily impurity could be transmitted through contact.
In this Gospel scene, the suffering woman touches Jesus...
and Jesus is not portrayed as becoming polluted.
Instead, healing goes from Him to her.
She reaches toward holiness...
and holiness restores her.
That is Jesus.
And suddenly the question is no longer merely:
“Why did somebody have to wash after touching a menstruating woman's bed?”
A deeper question begins to emerge:
How can unclean human beings ever draw near to a perfectly holy God?
That question reaches far beyond menstruation.
Because you may never have touched that ancient Israelite bed.
But you know what it is to need cleansing.
You know what it is to have something you wish nobody knew.
The browser history.
The affair.
The addiction.
The resentment.
The secret messages.
The lies.
The pride.
The years spent pretending.
The prayer life that quietly disappeared.
The compromise everyone else calls harmless.
The shame you learned to hide behind church language.
Some stains cannot be removed in a shower.
Some guilt survives every attempt at self-improvement.
Some nights you can wash your face, change your clothes, climb into a clean bed...
and still feel dirty inside.
That is where this ancient language begins pointing us toward something greater.
The New Testament book of Hebrews looks back at the old covenant system of purification and then asks, in effect:
If those rites dealt with ceremonial purification, how much more can the blood of Christ cleanse the conscience?
That is the Gospel.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad people behave more respectably.
He came for people who cannot cleanse themselves.
People like us.
The scandal of Christianity is not that good people finally became good enough for God.
The scandal is grace.
The innocent One took the place of the guilty.
The Holy One welcomed sinners.
The spotless Lamb carried sin.
The One who had no sin went to a cross surrounded by sinners and died for sinners.
Then He rose.
And now the invitation is not:
“Clean yourself enough and perhaps God will tolerate you.”
It is:
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop hiding.
Bring Him what you keep trying to conceal.
The Gospel does not tell you that sin is imaginary.
It tells you something infinitely better:
sin is real...
and Christ's grace is greater.
This is where we must make another distinction.
Menstruation was not moral sin.
Ritual impurity was not identical to wickedness.
We should never use Leviticus 15 to shame women for the bodies God gave them.

But the entire biblical drama of holiness, cleansing, sacrifice, priesthood, access, blood, and sanctuary prepares us to understand how astonishing it is that sinful humanity can finally approach God through Jesus Christ.
Hebrews says believers have confidence to enter God's presence by the blood of Jesus.
Think about that.
Leviticus teaches you not to treat holiness casually.
The Gospel does not make God less holy.
The Gospel reveals the staggering cost by which sinners are brought near to that holiness.
Jesus did not lower God's standard until we could crawl over it.
He fulfilled what we could never fulfill and gave Himself for us.
That is why Christianity is not fundamentally a self-cleaning program.
You do not scrub your soul until God loves you.
You come to Christ because while you could never rescue yourself, mercy came looking for you.
Maybe that is why the woman in Mark 5 feels so painfully familiar.
She had tried.
And tried.
And tried.
And eventually she reached the place where her hope was no longer:
“I can fix myself.”
Her hope became:
“If I can just get to Jesus.”
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You have promised God you would stop.
Then did it again.
You told everybody you were okay.
You weren't.
You posted Scripture while privately falling apart.
You smiled in church while fighting something nobody in the room could see.
Maybe you have even begun wondering whether Jesus would still want you if everything hidden became visible.
Look again at the trembling woman.
Jesus already knew.
And He called her daughter.
That does not mean Jesus excuses sin.
The same Christ who forgives calls us to repentance, obedience, holiness, and a transformed life.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace breaks chains.
Grace tells the truth about our condition and then refuses to leave us there.
So maybe tonight your prayer does not need to sound impressive.
Maybe it simply needs to be honest.
“Jesus, I need You.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, cleanse what I cannot cleanse.”
“Jesus, bring me home.”
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail.
But you can take one small step out of secrecy.
Someone else reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person still fighting.
Someone may pray for you.
Someone may finally confess to God because your honesty gave them courage to become honest too.
And if you know someone who has been wounded by the idea that the Bible teaches women are inherently dirty because of menstruation, share this with them.
Not to win an argument.
To remove a burden Scripture never asked them to carry.
Because eventually someone will ask you why Leviticus calls menstruation “unclean,” and you will want to remember the difference between ritual impurity and moral guilt.
But please remember something even more important.
The point of understanding Scripture is not merely becoming the person in the room who knows the Hebrew word.
Knowledge that never leads us toward Christ can simply make us proud in another language.
The goal is Jesus.
Always Jesus.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, return to Christ, repent, heal, grow, or put difficult passages back into their biblical context, you can also help this work continue.
We are not selling God's favor.
Biblical giving must never be manipulated.
But voluntary financial support can absolutely be an act of Christian generosity and stewardship when it is given freely, prayerfully, and for the advancement of Gospel work.
And sometimes glorifying God looks remarkably ordinary.
Someone writes.
Someone studies.
Someone gives.
Someone shares.
Someone prays.
And God uses all of it.
Pray.
Read.
Grow.

One share may put this truth in front of the woman who has carried unnecessary religious shame for twenty years. One tag may reach the believer quietly losing faith because nobody ever explained the difficult passages. One comment may encourage someone who thought they were fighting alone.
Because after all the Hebrew...
after the washing...
after the bed...
after the blood...
after twelve years of suffering...
after the trembling woman reached through the crowd...
we arrive at the truth we needed from the beginning.
The God who taught Israel that holiness must never be treated casually is the same God who, in Christ, made a way for sinners to draw near.
The woman reached for Jesus because she believed touching Him could change everything.
She was right.
And maybe that is the part you need to remember tonight.
Your deepest stain is not stronger than the Savior who still calls broken people closer.
